newsitem.title: BULGARIA: New Bulgarian president starts work on crisis.
newsitem.headline: New Bulgarian president starts work on crisis.

text.p: Bulgaria's new president starts work on Thursday in a country overwhelmed by political and economic crisis.

Petar Stoyanov took office on Wednesday in a colourful religious and military ceremony as the Socialist Party threatened to counter opposition protests with mass marches of its own unless it is allowed to form a new cabinet.
The president is usually a figurehead but Stoyanov must meet leaders of the Socialists and the opposition to seek a way forward and head off the risk of fresh violence.
Opposition rallies have been demanding for 16 days that the Socialists -- who formed the last government and still have a majority in parliament -- make way for a quick election.
In response, the ex-communist ruling party on Wednesday approved potentially explosive counter-protests by supporters around the country.

"It will be a funny sight -- red grannies rallying against Bulgarian students," said Yordan Sokolov, parliamentary leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces, referring to the Bulgarian Socialist Party's mostly elderly supporters.
"When this is over, the BSP will be history," he told the daily opposition rally, which gathered about 18,000 people.

The Socialists have offered elections in December, a year ahead of schedule, but in the meantime they want to form a new cabinet to take over from prime minister Zhan Videnov, who resigned on December 21. The UDF wants elections in March.
Students staged a symbolic funeral for the Socialists at the mausoleum of Bulgarian communist hero Georgi Dimitrov.
Weeping women prostrated themselves on a coffin draped with a red communist flag as a band played funeral marches.
One banner bore tables showing the lev's decline against the dollar to make a professor's monthly salary worth the equivalent of $35.

On the Socialist side, Valery Radev, regional party leader from the mining town of Bobov Dol, near Sofia, told reporters counter-protests could start immediately and would continue until the new president gave the Socialists a mandate to form a government.
Counter-rallies by supporters of neighbouring Serbia's Socialist President Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade on December 24 led to clashes between demonstrators and riot police.
Stoyanov, elected on the opposition ticket in November, took over command of the army from outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev at a parade outside the presidency.
He then received the blessing of the Orthodox church in the first religious ceremony for a new head of state since Boris III became king in October 1918.
The president cancelled the usual champagne reception as inappropriate at a time when hundreds of thousands of Bulgarians are hungry.

Stoyanov, a lawyer who specialises in divorce cases, backed opposition calls for early elections at his swearing-in ceremony last Sunday in the parliament, which was besieged and ransacked by demonstrators on January 10.

Under its post-communist constitution, Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic whose president is a mainly ceremonial figure, but one of his tasks is to ask the prime minister nominated by the largest parliamentary group to form a government.
Zhelev refused to ask the Bulgarian Socialist Party to form a government in the present explosive atmosphere, but Stoyanov has said he is prepared to do as the constitution requires.
Sokolov appeared to confirm fears that this might only heighten tension in the Balkan country of 8.4 million people.

"At our meeting with the president we shall suggest that he should give a mandate to the Socialists as soon as possible because we are ready for a general strike and we are going to sweep them out once and for all," he said.
Trade unions have warned of a general strike, but warning strikes have not won universal support.
